Title: Resolution of Singularities
Authors: Edward Bierstone, Pierre D. Milman
Date: Thu Sep 25 14:00:53 1997

This article is an exposition of an elementary constructive proof of canonical resolution of singularities in characteristic zero, presented in detail in Invent. Math. 128 (1997), 207-302. We define a new local invariant and get an algorithm for canonical desingularization by successively blowing up its maximum loci. The invariant can be described by local computations that provide equations for the centres of blowing up. We describe the origin of our approach and present the proof (in the hypersurface case) in parallel with a worked example.

Canonical desingularization in characteristic zero by blowing up the maximum strata of a local invariant (https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9508005)
【turn147473academia1】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 31.2 years ago; Title: Canonical desingularization in characteristic zero by blowing up the maximum strata of a local invariantAuthors: Edward Bierstone, Pierre Milman
Title: Canonical desingularization in characteristic zero by blowing up the maximum strata of a local invariant
Authors: Edward Bierstone, Pierre Milman
Date: Tue Aug 15 16:28:53 1995

This article contains an elementary constructive proof of resolution of singularities in characteristic zero. Our proof applies in particular to schemes of finite type and to analytic spaces (so we recover the great theorems of Hironaka). We introduce a discrete local invariant $\inv_X (a)$ whose maximum locus determines a smooth centre of blowing up, leading to desingularization. To define $\inv_X$, we need only to work with a category of local-ringed spaces $X=(|X|,{\cal O}_X)$ satisfying certain natural conditions. If $a\in |X|$, then $\inv_X(a)$ depends only on $\widehat{\cal O}_{X,a}$. More generally, $\inv_X(a)$ is defined inductively after any sequence of blowings-up whose centres have only normal crossings with respect to the exceptional divisors and lie in the constant loci of $\inv_X(\cdot)$. The paper is self-contained and includes detailed examples. One of our goals is that the reader understand the desingularization theorem, rather than simply ``know'' it is true.

Desingularization algorithms I. Role of exceptional divisors (https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0207098)
【turn147473academia2】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 24.2 years ago; Authors: Edward Bierstone, Pierre D.Milman ... The article is about a "desingularization principle" common to various canonical desingularization algorithms in characteristic zero, and the roles played by the exceptional divisors in the underlying local construction.
Title: Desingularization algorithms I. Role of exceptional divisors
Authors: Edward Bierstone, Pierre D. Milman
Date: Thu Jul 11 20:04:46 2002

The article is about a "desingularization principle" common to various canonical desingularization algorithms in characteristic zero, and the roles played by the exceptional divisors in the underlying local construction. We compare algorithms of the authors and of Villamayor and his collaborators, distinguishing between the fundamental effect of the way the exceptional divisors are used, and different theorems obtained because of flexibility allowed in the choice of "input data". We show how the meaning of "invariance" of the desingularization invariant, and the efficiency of the algorithm depend on the notion of "equivalence" of collections of local data used in the inductive construction.

Q-universal desingularization (https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.3580)
【turn147473academia3】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 17.4 years ago; Authors: Edward Bierstone, Pierre D.Milman, Michael Temkin ... We prove that the algorithm for desingularization of algebraic varieties in characteristic zero of the first two authors is functorial with respect to regular morphisms.
Title: Q-universal desingularization
Authors: Edward Bierstone, Pierre D. Milman, Michael Temkin
Date: Thu May 21 23:06:51 2009

We prove that the algorithm for desingularization of algebraic varieties in characteristic zero of the first two authors is functorial with respect to regular morphisms. For this purpose, we show that, in characteristic zero, a regular morphism with connected affine source can be factored into a smooth morphism, a ground-field extension and a generic-fibre embedding. Every variety of characteristic zero admits a regular morphism to a Q-variety. The desingularization algorithm is therefore Q-universal or absolute in the sense that it is induced from its restriction to varieties over Q. As a consequence, for example, the algorithm extends functorially to localizations and Henselizations of varieties.

summands in the tensor powers of representations of finite groups, over a field of arbitrary characteristic. In

solution to the growth problems in terms of the character table. We also provide code used to compute our
formulas.

Characteristic classes of Borel orbits of square-zero (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.03598)
【turn147473search6】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 2.1 years ago; Thus the theory is available for varieties in characteristic zero. ... the localization theorem computation may be reduced to local calculus of power series. ... ing to [6] the Demazure-Lusztig operations permute the motivic Chern classes of Schubert varieties.
We are primarily interested in the characteristic classes. One can think about characteristic classes
as a deformation of the notion of the fundamental class, as advertised in a review article [39]. We will
focus on the invariants listed below. They are of cohomological nature and live in Borel equivariant
cohomology or in equivariant K-theory. We will consider the equivariant theories for the maximal
torus.
• The fundamental classes in equivariant cohomology and equivariant K-theory serve as a starting
point, as well as an occasion to compare our approach with classical Schubert calculus.
• The Chern-Schwartz-MacPherson classes are the invariants of singular varieties having good co-
variant functorial properties. Their existence was conjectured by Grothendieck and Verdier. The
ﬁrst functorial construction was given by MacPherson [29]. It demands possibility of resolving
singularities. Thus the theory is available for varieties in characteristic zero. In a series of papers
Aluﬃ(e.g. [2, 3, 4]) computed many examples, gave an alternative deﬁnition and connected this
theory with various problems in enumerative geometry. An equivariant version was introduced
by Ohmoto [35, 45].
• The χy-genus deﬁned by Hirzebruch for smooth varieties admits an extension for singular vari-
eties and the underlying homology class was deﬁned in [10]. An equivariant version (especially
for torus action) were deﬁned and studied in [46]. A need and proﬁts from introducing equiv-
ariant version is clear when one deals with classical singular varieties like Schubert varieties. By
the localization theorem computation may be reduced to local calculus of power series. The K-
theoretic counterpart of the Hirzebruch class seems to be more natural for problems originating
from representation theory. The deﬁnition was given in [10] and the equivariant version was
introduced in [18, 6].
The structure allowing to compute the characteristic classes of Schubert varieties in the general-
ized ﬂag variety G/B serves as the model situation. The equivariant cohomology and K-theory with
respect to the maximal torus T ⊂B admit actions of the Demazure-Lusztig-type operations.

L22: 【8†Lemma 10.110.9.】 Let $R \to S$ be a local homomorphism of local Noetherian rings. Assume that $R \to S$ is flat and that $S$ is regular. Then $R$ is regular.
L23: Proof. Let $\mathfrak m \subset R$ be the maximal ideal and let $\kappa = R/\mathfrak m$ be the residue field. Let $d = \dim S$. Choose any resolution $F_\bullet \to \kappa $ with each $F_ i$ a finite free $R$-module. Set $K_ d = \mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}(F_{d - 1} \to F_{d - 2})$. By flatness of $R \to S$ the complex $0 \to K_ d \otimes _ R S \to F_{d - 1} \otimes _ R S \to \ldots \to F_0 \otimes _ R S \to \kappa \otimes _ R S \to 0$ is still exact.
L24: Because the global dimension of $S$ is $d$, see Proposition 【14†10.110.1】, we see that $K_ d \otimes _ R S$ is a finite free $S$-module (see also Lemma 【15†10.109.3】). By Lemma 【16†10.78.6】 we see that $K_ d$ is a finite free $R$-module. Hence $\kappa $ has finite projective dimension and $R$ is regular by Proposition 【17†10.110.5】. $\square$

L23: 【8†Lemma 10.112.8.】 Let $R \to S$ be a local homomorphism of local Noetherian rings. Assume
L24: 
L25:   1. $R$ is regular,
L26: 
L27:   2. $S/\mathfrak m_ RS$ is regular, and
L28: 
L29:   3. $R \to S$ is flat.
L30: 
L31: Then $S$ is regular.
L32: Proof. By Lemma 【10†10.112.7】 we have $\dim (S) = \dim (R) + \dim (S/\mathfrak m_ RS)$. Pick generators $x_1, \ldots , x_ d \in \mathfrak m_ R$ with $d = \dim (R)$, and pick $y_1, \ldots , y_ e \in \mathfrak m_ S$ which generate the maximal ideal of $S/\mathfrak m_ RS$ with $e = \dim (S/\mathfrak m_ RS)$. Then we see that $x_1, \ldots , x_ d, y_1, \ldots , y_ e$ are elements which generate the maximal ideal of $S$ and $e + d = \dim (S)$. $\square$

L22: 【8†Lemma 74.13.1.】 Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an invertible $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module. Let $\{ g_ i : Y_ i \to Y\} _{i \in I}$ be an fpqc covering. Let $f_ i : X_ i \to Y_ i$ be the base change of $f$ and let $\mathcal{L}_ i$ be the pullback of $\mathcal{L}$ to $X_ i$. The following are equivalent
L23: 
L24:   1. $\mathcal{L}$ is ample on $X/Y$, and
L25: 
L26:   2. $\mathcal{L}_ i$ is ample on $X_ i/Y_ i$ for every $i \in I$.
L27: Proof. The implication (1) $\Rightarrow $ (2) follows from Divisors on Spaces, Lemma 【14†71.14.3】. Assume (2). To check $\mathcal{L}$ is ample on $X/Y$ we may work étale locally on $Y$, see Divisors on Spaces, Lemma 【15†71.14.6】. Thus we may assume that $Y$ is a scheme and then we may in turn assume each $Y_ i$ is a scheme too, see Topologies on Spaces, Lemma 【16†73.9.5】. In other words, we may assume that $\{ Y_ i \to Y\} $ is an fpqc covering of schemes.
L28: By Divisors on Spaces, Lemma 【17†71.14.4】 we see that $X_ i \to Y_ i$ is representable (i.e., $X_ i$ is a scheme), quasi-compact, and separated. Hence $f$ is quasi-compact and separated by Lemmas 【18†74.11.1】 and 【19†74.11.18】. This means that $\mathcal{A} = \bigoplus _{d \geq 0} f_*\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ is a quasi-coherent graded $\mathcal{O}_ Y$-algebra (Morphisms of Spaces, Lemma 【20†67.11.2】).
L29: Moreover, the formation of $\mathcal{A}$ commutes with flat base change by Cohomology of Spaces, Lemma 【21†69.11.2】. In particular, if we set $\mathcal{A}_ i = \bigoplus _{d \geq 0} f_{i, *}\mathcal{L}_ i^{\otimes d}$ then we have $\mathcal{A}_ i = g_ i^*\mathcal{A}$.
